video.title: The Credit Card Side Hustle No One Talks About

summary: Colin Stroud describes Go Somewhere, a business that helps owners improve credit card rewards and helps travellers book trips with points. He grew it from a LinkedIn-led side hustle into a full-time business, with fixed-fee consulting, trip research and credit-card affiliate income. He says AI tools help with research and operations, while customers still value human advice and support. The model is learnable and mostly online, but its acquisition depends heavily on LinkedIn and its core services still require human expertise.

speakers.name: Colin Stroud
speakers.description: Founder of Go Somewhere and credit card rewards consultant.

ideas.name: Credit card rewards consulting for business owners
ideas.one_liner: For a fixed fee, review a business owner's spending, recommend a points-earning card strategy, help implement it and include planning for a future trip.
ideas.business_model: One-time fixed-fee consulting package; affiliate commissions are an additional revenue stream.
ideas.customer: Business owners with substantial card spending, including construction and other local businesses. Colin says his target clients spend at least $20,000 a month on cards; many have significant spending but little time or interest in optimizing rewards.
ideas.problem: Owners may use cards that return relatively few points for their spending and may not know how to transfer or redeem rewards effectively.
ideas.offer: A 75-minute consultation reviewing personal and business spending, a written credit card rewards strategy, implementation help by email or text, and planning for the client's next major trip using points.

price_points.label: Earlier fee to talk to Colin
Hypothetical price for a basic zero-to-one strategy, suggested by Colin

pricing.notes: The main current offer is $875. The $400 figure is an example of what a beginner might charge for a simpler strategy, not a stated current price.

acquisition_channels.details: LinkedIn is Colin's main source of clients. He posts educational content and examples of points deals; he says client acquisition has been inbound and organic.

quote.text: I'm posting one, two times a day, six days a week, and LinkedIn has been my best friend, for sure.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

acquisition_channels.details: He also shares content and affiliate links with clients and his newsletter audience. Most of his email subscribers came from LinkedIn.

quote.text: I've got 7,000 email subscribers. So I think I could sell there.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

ideas.delivery: Colin conducts a discovery call, researches the client's personal and business spending, writes a recommended card strategy, discusses it on a live consultation, and provides follow-up help by email or text. A future trip plan is included, with the client contacting him when ready to travel.
unit_economics_claims: Colin charges $875 for the one-time business-owner package.
Colin said his software subscriptions and similar costs were about $100, with almost no other costs at that point.

A consultation client can require a discovery call, research, a 75-minute consultation, follow-up writing and potentially later trip research; he said the trip portion can take from 20 minutes to four hours.
Colin said his revenue reached $13,000 in November 2024, $231,000 gross in 2025, and $89,000 year to date by April 30, 2026.
He said he had about $40,000 in expenses in 2025, including software, travel and contractors.
tools: Credit card issuer websites and rewards programmes
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Colin said ongoing software subscriptions and similar costs were about $100, but did not specify the period.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Colin said he first made $1,000 in a month in March 2024 and started the business as a side hustle.

acquisition.how: AI could help research and draft posts, but acquiring clients currently depends on Colin creating useful LinkedIn content and building trust with a human audience.

onboarding.how: The client completes a discovery call and shares personal and business spending details; the transcript does not describe automated intake.

delivery.how: The core value is Colin's review, live advice and written recommendations. AI may assist research, but the offer is explicitly sold as a human consultation.

billing.how: A fixed fee is straightforward to charge through routine payment software, but no billing tool or automated process is stated.

support.how: Implementation help comes through email and text, and follow-up trip assistance can require additional human research.

uk_applicability.notes: The online consulting and content model can operate in the UK, but card products, rewards programmes and transfer partners differ by country. UK advice and affiliate promotions may also require careful review of financial-promotion and consumer-credit rules.

risks: The service relies on specialist knowledge of card terms and rewards programmes that can change.
The included trip-planning support can create open-ended work months after the original sale, making the effective hourly return unpredictable.
Colin says LinkedIn has been his easy source of clients and that he has little outbound-sales experience, creating platform concentration risk.
In the UK, credit-card recommendations and affiliate promotions need careful review for applicable financial-promotion and consumer-credit requirements.
A client may expect a specific award redemption that is not actually available when they are ready to book.

ideas.name: Points-based trip research and booking assistance
ideas.one_liner: Research award travel options for people with points, then charge a deposit and a flat fee based on the trip's complexity.
ideas.business_model: Deposit to start, followed by a flat trip-research fee when a booking is completed.
ideas.customer: People anywhere who have credit card points and want help finding flights or hotels, particularly higher-income travellers with large point balances and complicated itineraries.
ideas.problem: Travellers may have many points but find it confusing and time-consuming to locate useful award availability and book a trip.
ideas.offer: The customer submits a website form describing their points, destination and travel preferences. The team researches award options, helps find a deal and assists with booking.

pricing.model: Deposit plus flat fee based on trip scope.

acquisition_channels.details: A customer can visit the Go Somewhere website and submit a free form. The transcript does not specify how most trip-research customers discover the site.

Colin says two contractors now handle about 90% of the trip research. He uses an AI-supported award search tool and a custom CRM and dashboard built with Lovable.

acquisition.how: The website form can accept inbound requests continuously, while social content can generate demand. The source of most form traffic and any paid acquisition process are not stated.

onboarding.how: A website form and a deposit can make intake and starting work mostly software-driven, although requests need scope review.

delivery.how: Seats.aero and AI can speed up award searches, but the transcript says human contractors do most of the research and the team helps clients book.

billing.how: A fixed deposit and scope-based fee could be collected with routine payment tools, but no payment system or automation is stated.

support.how: Trip requests require human judgment, changing award availability and follow-up with customers; contractors handle much of the research.

uk_applicability.notes: The online trip-research model can serve UK customers, but award availability, card transfer partners, fees and airline or hotel programmes vary by market. UK card rewards expertise would be needed.

The business depends on contractors with points expertise and on third-party award-search tools.

ideas.name: Credit-card affiliate referrals
ideas.one_liner: Share bank or card affiliate links with clients and an audience, earning a commission when someone signs up.
ideas.business_model: Affiliate commissions from credit card referrals.
ideas.customer: Card issuers seeking applicants; the audience consists of clients, newsletter readers and social media followers considering cards.
ideas.problem: Card issuers want to acquire customers, while business owners and travellers may need to find a card suited to their spending and rewards goals.
ideas.offer: Recommend or share affiliate links for relevant premium credit cards through client communications, a newsletter and social media.

pricing.model: Commission per approved or completed card referral; exact terms are not stated.

price_points.label: Colin's general estimate of potential commission

pricing.notes: Colin says a premium-card referral can easily make $400, and says affiliate links have become a key part of his revenue. The transcript does not state his actual commission schedule.

acquisition_channels.details: Colin shares links with clients and in his newsletter.

quote.text: sharing affiliate links to clients in my newsletter and even on social media.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

acquisition_channels.details: He also posts or shares affiliate links through social media, including LinkedIn.

ideas.delivery: The affiliate link directs the potential cardholder to the issuer. Colin may provide context through his consulting or content, but the card issuer handles the application and card product.
unit_economics_claims: Colin says a premium-card referral can easily generate $400.
He says affiliate links have become a key part of his revenue.

acquisition.how: Links can be placed in inbound content and newsletters, but earning attention and trust still requires audience-building.

onboarding.how: A referral link can send applicants to an issuer's online application flow with little manual onboarding.

delivery.how: The issuer handles the card application and product delivery; Colin's role is to choose and share relevant links.

billing.how: Affiliate tracking and commissions are usually handled by the issuer or affiliate platform, but Colin does not name the programme or its process.

support.how: Questions about which card suits a customer may require individual human advice and careful explanation.

uk_applicability.notes: Affiliate referrals can operate in the UK, but available card products and issuer programmes differ. UK financial-promotion and affiliate-disclosure requirements need to be reviewed.

risks: Affiliate income depends on card issuer programmes, approval rules and terms that may change.
A commission can create a conflict of interest if recommendations are not clearly separated from commercial incentives.
Colin says card banks dislike the term 'hacking' when he uses affiliate links, so language and issuer rules matter.
UK affiliate links and credit-card recommendations require review for applicable disclosure and financial-promotion rules.

tactics.name: Validate demand by doing and sharing a real award-search example
steps: Choose a specific points deal and research how it can be booked.
Call the airline if needed; Colin says he spent about five hours on a Turkish Airlines-to-Hawaii example and was on hold for about an hour.
Get as far as confirming the booking path without spending money if you are practising.
Post the research and what you learned on LinkedIn, accurately saying whether you booked the trip.
Use audience response as evidence of interest; Colin says his post received almost 100,000 impressions with about 1,000 followers.

quote.text: Not for a real client just for me. Didn't book it. I got on the phone with the agent. I was on the hold like an hour.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Use LinkedIn content for inbound demand
steps: Publish useful points and rewards content one or two times a day, six days a week, as Colin says he did.
Share practical research and examples rather than relying on outbound sales.
Build an email list from the audience so there is a channel to reach people if social distribution changes.

quote.text: I've almost never done any kind of outbound marketing that's been 100% inbound organic, just from content.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Start with spending and earning rate, not card perks
steps: Ask how much the customer spends and where that spending occurs.
Compare the points earned on those categories before weighing lounge access or insurance benefits.
Recommend a simple card strategy that fits the spending pattern and explain how to implement it.

quote.text: stop focusing on the benefits of your card and start thinking about how much it's earning.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Scope trip research with a form, deposit and complexity-based fee
steps: Collect the traveller's points balance, destination, cabin and trip requirements in a website form.
Take a deposit to start work.
Quote a flat fee based on trip complexity, with multi-city and larger-family trips costing more.
Collect the remaining fee once the trip is booked.

quote.text: Anybody on the internet in the world could come to my website, fill out a form. And it's free to fill out the form.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Systematize research and delegate trip work
steps: Use an award-search tool to search multiple programmes rather than checking airline sites one at a time.
Track trips through a custom CRM and dashboard built with Lovable.
Hire experienced points researchers to handle most of the research while retaining oversight and client contact.

quote.text: So custom CRM, custom dashboard, really, really cool. So in terms of delivering that service, it's all done through AI by humans.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Learn through free resources and practise before taking clients
steps: Study points blogs and free courses, including The Daily Drop resources Colin recommends.
Practise researching an itinerary using your own points or by stopping before payment.
Build a truthful sample case study from the research and distinguish a researched example from a completed booking.

quote.text: Luckily, you can practice on yourself. Like you can go book fake trips, basically. You can get all the way to the booking stage and stop.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

tactics.name: Keep a simple fixed-fee core offer
steps: State the package price clearly before work begins.
Keep the scope easy to understand: consultation, written strategy, implementation help and one trip plan.
Track the later trip work because it can vary substantially and affect the effective hourly return.

quote.text: I charge flat fees. So I say it, yeah, it's what you want. This is exactly how much it costs. I keep it really simple.
quote.speaker: Colin Stroud

lessons.lesson: Validate interest by doing the work, sharing what you learned and observing whether people respond before building a large operation.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is a first-hand operator and describes his offers, acquisition channel, delivery workflow, contractor use and several business figures. The numbers are self-reported, the transcript is local Whisper output with apparent misheard card names and prices, and the interview does not independently verify the claims.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Colin says bank affiliate links are a key part of his revenue and that he shares them with clients and his audience. The host also reads a Beehiiv sponsor advertisement with a discount offer.
